Human beings, meanwhile, were limited to knowledge gained through the senses and to the direct, purely empirical knowledge that sensory experience could provide.
In this way, Islam created a reciprocal relationship between knowledge and faith.
Within this framework, rational knowledge available to human beings could go no further than using sensory knowledge to support religious belief.
It was therefore natural for us to conclude that Islam closed the way to intellectual debate over matters of faith and questions concerning the world beyond nature.
Islamic texts do not leave this conclusion unsupported.
The Qurʾan and sayings attributed to the Prophet contain passages that either forbid or discourage debate over such questions.

But when Arab thought found this route to further development blocked, it turned in another direction: toward independent legal reasoning based on personal judgment in applying the general rules and principles of Islamic law.

It followed this path until historical conditions made it possible to reopen the first path as well—the path of rational debate over questions of faith and over the metaphysical nature of the universe.
After the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, political and sectarian struggles became more intense. From those struggles came the living seeds of philosophical thought.
Those seeds then developed naturally within Arab-Islamic life until, in the ninth century CE, they produced what became known as Arab philosophy.
C — The Age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs
We devoted Chapter Three of Part One to the most important historical developments of this period.
These developments created the setting in which different forms of religious conflict and later political and sectarian conflict took shape.
This conflict matters to our study because, once the Umayyad period began, much of it developed into an intellectual and “ideological” struggle.

Other intellectual and ideological currents either became part of this struggle or developed alongside it. These included the Muʿtazila, the current represented by the ideas of al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, the Qadariyya, and others.
Chapter Three also examined another major historical development of the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs: the Arab conquests, which began during the rule of the second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb.
The importance of these conquests for our study lies in their major role in placing Arab thought on the path that would eventually lead toward scientific and philosophical thinking.
The conquests created the historical conditions for social and cultural interaction between the Arabs and the peoples of the conquered countries.
That interaction later played an enormous role in shaping the distinctive features of Arab culture and Arab thought.
It also brought together internal and external cultural elements, and Arab philosophy was one of the products of that combination.
Our discussion in this chapter took place within the framework of all these historical developments.
Within that same framework, we can now present the main conclusions reached during the chapter.
First: The struggle over the caliphate that broke out immediately after the Prophet’s death released a form of social conflict that had previously taken different forms during his lifetime.
At the beginning of Islam, the main conflict had been between two sides: the new religion and its followers on one side, and the wealthy leaders of Quraysh and their traditions on the other.
Later, after Islam spread and defeated its opponents in Mecca following the Hijra, the main conflict changed.
On one side stood the Helpers and the Emigrants. On the other stood tribes that continued to hold on to their pre-Islamic traditions and social arrangements.
After the Prophet’s death, however, the main contradiction shifted again.
This time, the opposing sides were Muslims themselves.
The caliphate, as a religious office, appeared to be the main issue around which the conflict revolved.
Behind it, however, lay social motives and the desire to control the political power that came with the office.
One striking fact is that the Ridda Wars, which occupied the Muslims immediately after the Prophet’s death, did not replace the caliphate as the central issue in this conflict.

Even the wars of conquest, which began moving beyond the Arabian Peninsula under the second caliph, ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb, while the Ridda Wars had not yet fully ended, failed to shift the main conflict away from the question of the caliphate.
Another striking point is the remarkable success Muslims achieved in both the Ridda Wars and the wars of conquest even though the central conflict over the caliphate remained unresolved.
The reason was that the different Muslim groups shared certain social interests: suppressing the rebellion within Arabia and expanding Arab territory beyond the peninsula.
These shared interests helped push the dispute over the caliphate into the form of a religious disagreement over the nature of the office itself.
Was the caliphate a divine office, or was it a worldly political office whose holder should be chosen by Muslims themselves?
Behind this religious form, however, we saw a deeper social difference.
The idea of the caliphate as a divine office expressed, in our view, the hopes of ordinary people for social justice.
The idea of the caliphate as a worldly political office expressed the interests of the wealthy aristocracy.
This religious form of the conflict remained clearly visible on the surface of events only during the reigns of the first two caliphs, Abu Bakr and ʿUmar.
Second: Beginning with the reign of the third caliph, ʿUthmān, the religious form of the struggle over the caliphate increasingly revealed its social and political basis.
One important reason was the conduct of the governors who represented the caliph in the provinces under his rule.
Their main concern became personal enrichment, often through outright seizure.
They took possession of other people’s land and imposed heavy taxes on the population.
Discontent with these policies grew and accumulated in different regions until it developed into a social revolt.
Groups of ordinary people came in delegations from several provinces to Mecca and Medina to protest to Caliph ʿUthmān and demand that he give up the caliphate.
When he refused, the delegations surrounded him in his house, and he was eventually killed.
Some of the political factions struggling for power in Mecca and Medina had played a part in pushing the revolt toward this outcome.
After ʿUthmān’s death, some of these same political forces used his killing as a pretext to redirect the legitimate social revolt against unjust governors.
The political struggle was driven back toward its original center—the struggle over the caliphate itself—but now in a much sharper and more violent form.
This directly led to a series of “internal” wars among Muslim leaders.
These included the Battle of the Camel in Basra, fought between ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib on one side and Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr, led by the Prophet’s wife ʿĀʾisha, on the other.
They also included the Battle of Ṣiffīn between the armies of ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya.
Then came the wars of the Kharijites, who had broken away from ʿAlī’s ranks at Ṣiffīn and formed a new party that fought both ʿAlī and Muʿāwiya after declaring both of them unbelievers.
Third: The wars of conquest did not unfold separately from the “internal” events created by these political struggles among Muslim leaders.
The policies followed by the conquerors in the territories under their rule were strongly affected by the course of these conflicts.
Their effects spread through the conquered lands, and Muslims there divided between supporters of one side and supporters of another.
ʿAlī had a large following in Iraq and Iran, while Muʿāwiya’s supporters were dominant in Syria.
In Egypt, factional loyalties were less visible among the ordinary population.
They appeared more clearly, however, in the views of jurists and transmitters of the Prophet’s sayings among the Companions and their followers.
In other words, the division was strongest among educated circles and people known for forming and expressing considered opinions.
Fourth: For most of the age of the Rightly Guided Caliphs, Arab rule in the conquered countries remained mainly military in character.
The conquerors built cities that were originally intended as bases for their armies, and the way they lived in these cities kept them separated from the lives of the local population.
This military character delayed the process of cultural and social interaction.
Later, as we shall see, that interaction would have enormous consequences for the development of Arab thought and Arab culture.
